hint: The FTC says: the derivative of $\int_a^x f(t) \, dt$ with respect to $x$ is just $f(x)$. No integrating needed.

hints.text: The FTC says: the derivative of $\int_a^x f(t) \, dt$ with respect to $x$ is just $f(x)$. No integrating needed.

explanation: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Part 1): if $g(x) = \int_a^x f(t) \, dt$, then $g'(x) = f(x)$.
Here $f(t) = t^2 + 1$, so $g'(x) = x^2 + 1$. The lower limit $1$ plays no role in the derivative.
$g'(2) = 2^2 + 1 = 5$. Meaning: as $x$ passes $2$, the accumulated area grows at $5$ units of area per unit of $x$ — the height of the curve there.

alternativeExplanations.title: The long way, to see why it works
steps: Differentiate: $g'(x) = x^2 + 1$. The constant $-\frac{4}{3}$ from the lower limit vanishes.
$g'(2) = 5$. The FTC lets you skip straight to this.
